items.title: A Visual Guide to Attention Kernels
items.abstract:
A Visual Guide to Attention Kernels was recorded as a Lightning Talk session at the 2026 AI Engineering Summit. The session focuses on serving and optimizing large models under real production constraints. The project referenced by this session is Dao-AILab/flash-attention. Programme notes describe the project as: the open-source flash-attention project, which the speaker uses as the reference implementation for the techniques shown on stage. The speaker combines architecture diagrams, production anecdotes, and benchmark results, and reserves time at the end for questions from practitioners.

The speaker frames serving as a scheduling problem: requests, KV cache blocks, batching windows, and hardware memory all compete for the same resources.

A detailed section covers cache reuse, prefix sharing, and eviction policies, with guidance on when the complexity of a shared cache pays for itself.

Continuous batching and paged attention are explained through production traces rather than benchmark charts, including the tail latency effects that appear when long and short requests mix.

Benchmarks are reported at the request level, with percentile latency, throughput under saturation, and memory headroom so that operators can reproduce the result.

The session contrasts speculative decoding, lookahead decoding, and draft-model approaches, noting that acceptance rates are workload dependent.

The speaker highlights easy wins first: better batching, fewer copies, tighter tokenizers, and honest load tests before investing in exotic kernels.

Method and measurement. The team used a staged rollout with canary traffic, automatic rollback, and a weekly review of quality regressions. Failure analysis is given as much time as the success story, including a list of assumptions that did not survive contact with real traffic. The speaker is explicit about the difference between microbenchmarks and end-to-end product measurements. A cost table compares tokens, latency, engineering hours, and operational risk for each option discussed.

Takeaways. The session ends with a short reading list and an invitation to contribute issues and reproduction scripts to the referenced project. Attendees should leave with a concrete checklist for reproducing the core result in their own environment. The team encourages readers to treat every generated artifact as untrusted until verified by a deterministic check. The final advice is to document the assumptions behind a benchmark, because those assumptions are what future maintainers will question.

Session context. Slides, recordings, and short notes accompany the session in the archive. The room was full, and the questions after the talk focused on deployment details rather than demos. The speaker used production incidents as teaching material and was candid about what failed before the final design.

The presenter noted that documentation quality often determines whether a technique is adopted, since most teams first encounter the idea through an internal write-up rather than the original paper.

The talk included a short retrospective on what the team would do differently if they started again with the same constraints.

Audience questions ranged from hardware selection to team structure, and the answers consistently returned to clarity of measurement.

The speaker drew a distinction between a demo that succeeds once and a system that succeeds repeatedly under noisy inputs.

During the audience discussion, one participant described a similar rollout that stalled because ownership was split across teams; the speaker recommended a single service owner for the end-to-end workflow.

The speaker answered a question about security by describing the permission model, the sandbox boundary, and the review process for sensitive actions.

The session included a brief discussion of privacy, including how long traces are retained and how user data is scrubbed before storage.

The presenter emphasized that tooling should make the safe path the easy path, because operators under pressure tend to take shortcuts.

A follow-up workshop covers the hands-on version of the same material, with exercises that rebuild a small end-to-end pipeline.

A comparison slide showed the same workload before and after the change, with percentile latencies rather than averages so that tail behavior was visible.

Several recommendations were framed as defaults that teams can start with and then relax only after measuring the tradeoff in their own environment.

The presentation closed with an open invitation to reproduce the benchmark and report divergence, since negative results are also useful.

items.title: Safety Filters for Open Models
items.abstract:
Safety Filters for Open Models was recorded as a Main Track session at the 2026 AI Engineering Summit. The session focuses on measurement, benchmarking, red-teaming, and guardrails for deployed models. The project referenced by this session is meta-llama/PurpleLlama. Programme notes describe the project as: the open-source PurpleLlama project, which the speaker uses as the reference implementation for the techniques shown on stage. The speaker combines architecture diagrams, production anecdotes, and benchmark results, and reserves time at the end for questions from practitioners.

Safety filters are evaluated on both false positives and false negatives, because over-blocking quietly destroys user trust and product metrics.

The speaker starts from the observation that evaluation is a product requirement, not a research afterthought, and that ambiguous metrics create false confidence.

The talk examines contamination, leakage, and benchmark saturation, with practical tests for detecting them before leaders rely on a score.

The session distinguishes offline quality checks, online guardrails, and incident review, showing how each catches different failures.

Red-teaming is presented as a continuous program with ownership, triage, and regression tests rather than a one-off exercise.

The closing segment connects evaluation results to release decisions and rollback criteria.

Method and measurement. Each experiment reports hardware, batch sizes, prompt templates, and evaluation settings so the audience can judge how far the result will transfer. A cost table compares tokens, latency, engineering hours, and operational risk for each option discussed. The speaker is explicit about the difference between microbenchmarks and end-to-end product measurements. The methodology section walks through the baseline, the instrumentation used to measure it, and the conditions under which the improvement appears.

Takeaways. The speaker recommends starting with the simplest configuration that satisfies the product requirement. A second takeaway is that observability and evaluation must be designed together with the feature. The team encourages readers to treat every generated artifact as untrusted until verified by a deterministic check. The session ends with a short reading list and an invitation to contribute issues and reproduction scripts to the referenced project.

items.title: Stateful Memory Services for Long-Horizon Agents
items.abstract:
Stateful Memory Services for Long-Horizon Agents was recorded as a Main Track session at the 2026 AI Engineering Summit. The session focuses on the engineering of reliable agents, tool use, orchestration, and state management. The project referenced by this session is mem0ai/mem0. Programme notes describe the project as: A memory layer service that gives agents persistent, personalized long-term memory with extraction, storage, and retrieval APIs. The speaker combines architecture diagrams, production anecdotes, and benchmark results, and reserves time at the end for questions from practitioners.

The talk closes with cost and latency accounting, showing where orchestration overhead dominates and how caching, batching, and concurrency limits change the economics of agent products.

Human-in-the-loop controls are treated as a first-class feature rather than an afterthought: approval gates, diff previews, and escalation policies are designed before the agent is deployed.

The team presents a checklist for reliability: deterministic tool adapters, idempotent actions, checkpointed state, and replayable transcripts for every long-running task.

Several examples show how to keep an agent grounded in an environment: sandboxed file systems, browser sessions, shell access, and structured observations that the model can verify.

The speaker opens with a taxonomy of agent runtimes: planners, executors, tool routers, memory services, and policy layers that decide when an autonomous loop should stop and ask for help.

Observability receives a full section. The speaker demonstrates span-level traces that connect a user request to each planning step, tool invocation, retry, and final artifact.

Method and measurement. The methodology section walks through the baseline, the instrumentation used to measure it, and the conditions under which the improvement appears. The speaker is explicit about the difference between microbenchmarks and end-to-end product measurements. A cost table compares tokens, latency, engineering hours, and operational risk for each option discussed. The session includes a short live debugging segment in which a deliberately broken configuration is diagnosed from traces.

Takeaways. A second takeaway is that observability and evaluation must be designed together with the feature. Questions about scale were answered with a reminder that the operational envelope matters more than the peak headline number. Attendees should leave with a concrete checklist for reproducing the core result in their own environment. The speaker recommends starting with the simplest configuration that satisfies the product requirement.

Session context. The presentation assumes familiarity with Python and basic model-serving concepts but does not require research experience. The speaker contrasted research prototypes with systems that must run unattended overnight and recover from partial failures. Examples were drawn from internal tools, customer-facing assistants, and open-source deployments.

The talk separates retrieval quality from memory quality: one is about finding evidence, the other about deciding what to keep and when to forget.

The speaker closes with guidance on building retrieval APIs that agents can call repeatedly without flooding context windows.

Memory services are evaluated on write amplification, retrieval precision, provenance, and the ability to delete user data safely.

Index design is covered in depth, including chunking, metadata filters, hybrid search, and reranking under tight latency budgets.

Evaluation for retrieval is framed with recall at k, grounded answer rate, and citation quality, not only similarity scores.

Several failure cases show retrieval systems confidently returning stale or contradictory evidence when freshness signals are missing.
